short_description.id: Lilith adalah sosok demonik dalam tradisi Jewish; kisah medieval menyebutnya istri pertama Adam, sedangkan penafsiran kata lilit dalam Isaiah masih diperdebatkan.
short_description.en: Lilith is a demonic figure in Jewish tradition. A medieval story presents her as Adam's first wife, while the interpretation of the word lilit in Isaiah remains debated.

long_description.id: Sumber Jewish menggambarkan Lilith sebagai demon malam. Kata lilit muncul dalam Isaiah 34:14, tetapi penafsirannya dapat menunjuk pada burung malam atau demon; karena itu, kemunculan kata tersebut tidak dapat begitu saja disamakan dengan seluruh legenda Lilith yang berkembang kemudian. Sumber ensiklopedis lama juga membandingkannya dengan nama-nama demon Assyrian.
long_description.en: Jewish sources describe Lilith as a night demon. The word lilit appears in Isaiah 34:14, but its interpretation may refer to a night bird or demon; the word should therefore not be equated with the full later Lilith legend. An older encyclopedia also compares her with names of Assyrian demons.

long_description.id: Dalam Alphabet of Ben Sira yang berasal dari sekitar abad kesembilan atau kesepuluh, Lilith digambarkan diciptakan bagi Adam, lalu bertengkar dan melarikan diri setelah mengucapkan nama ilahi. Cerita itu mengaitkannya dengan ancaman bagi bayi dan penggunaan nama malaikat pada jimat untuk melindungi mereka. Keterangan ini berasal dari kisah tersebut.
long_description.en: In the ninth or tenth century Alphabet of Ben Sira, Lilith is made for Adam, quarrels with him, and flees after speaking the divine name. The tale connects her with danger to infants and with angels' names on amulets to protect children. These details come from that work.

long_description.id: Teks Talmud juga mengaitkan Lilith dengan kegelapan dan seksualitas. Zohar kemudian menempatkannya sebagai istri Adam dan Satan dalam penafsiran mistik. Pada masa modern, sejumlah pembaca menafsirkan ulang Lilith sebagai lambang kebebasan perempuan.
long_description.en: Talmudic material also connects Lilith with darkness and sexuality. The Zohar later portrays her as wife of Adam and Satan in a mystical reading. In modern reinterpretations, some readers have made Lilith a symbol of women's freedom.

description.en: The Alphabet of Ben Sira has Lilith speak the divine name, fly, and flee.

long_description.id: Lilith (bahasa Ibrani: לִילִית‎ Lîlîṯ) adalah sebuah nama Ibrani bagi suatu sosok dalam mitologi Yahudi, yang dikembangkan paling awal dalam Talmud Babel, yang umumnya dianggap sebagian diturunkan dari semacam setan betina dalam kisah lebih kuno (līlīṯu) dalam agama Mesopotamia, sebagaimana ditemukan dalam teks kuneiform dari Sumer, Akkad, Asyur, dan Babel.
long_description.en: Lilith (; Hebrew: לִילִית, romanized: Līlīṯ; also spelled Lilit or Lilis) is a feminine figure in late-antique Mesopotamian and Jewish mythology. Lilith does not appear in the Hebrew Bible or any other biblical source, although the Hebrew word lilit appears in the Book of Isaiah, specifically in Isaiah 34:14. The meaning of this word is debated by scholars with interpretations ranging from a primordial she-demon to a night bird. The King James translation renders the term in this verse as "screech-owl". Based on medieval Jewish folklore, Lilith is said to have fled from the Garden of Eden because she did not want to submit to Adam. The earliest known mention of Lilith is in the Dead Sea Scrolls (4Q510-11), and afterwards in Mandaean and Jewish sources from late antiquity (300 AD onward), in historiolas – incantations that incorporate a short mythic story – that give partial descriptions of her. She is mentioned in the Babylonian Talmud (at Eruvin 100b, Niddah 24b, Shabbat 151b, Bava Batra 73a), and in the Zohar § Leviticus 19a as "a hot fiery female who first cohabited with man". Some rabbinic authorities, including Maimonides and Menachem Meiri, reject the existence of Lilith.

short_description.id: Lilith adalah sosok demonik dalam tradisi Jewish; kisah medieval menyebutnya istri pertama Adam, sedangkan penafsiran kata lilit dalam Isaiah masih diperdebatkan.
short_description.en: Lilith is a demonic figure in Jewish tradition. A medieval story presents her as Adam's first wife, while the interpretation of the word lilit in Isaiah remains debated.

long_description.id: Sumber Jewish menggambarkan Lilith sebagai demon malam. Kata lilit muncul dalam Isaiah 34:14, tetapi penafsirannya dapat menunjuk pada burung malam atau demon; karena itu, kemunculan kata tersebut tidak dapat begitu saja disamakan dengan seluruh legenda Lilith yang berkembang kemudian. Sumber ensiklopedis lama juga membandingkannya dengan nama-nama demon Assyrian.
long_description.en: Jewish sources describe Lilith as a night demon. The word lilit appears in Isaiah 34:14, but its interpretation may refer to a night bird or demon; the word should therefore not be equated with the full later Lilith legend. An older encyclopedia also compares her with names of Assyrian demons.

long_description.id: Dalam Alphabet of Ben Sira yang berasal dari sekitar abad kesembilan atau kesepuluh, Lilith digambarkan diciptakan bagi Adam, lalu bertengkar dan melarikan diri setelah mengucapkan nama ilahi. Cerita itu mengaitkannya dengan ancaman bagi bayi dan penggunaan nama malaikat pada jimat untuk melindungi mereka. Keterangan ini berasal dari kisah tersebut.
long_description.en: In the ninth or tenth century Alphabet of Ben Sira, Lilith is made for Adam, quarrels with him, and flees after speaking the divine name. The tale connects her with danger to infants and with angels' names on amulets to protect children. These details come from that work.

long_description.id: Teks Talmud juga mengaitkan Lilith dengan kegelapan dan seksualitas. Zohar kemudian menempatkannya sebagai istri Adam dan Satan dalam penafsiran mistik. Pada masa modern, sejumlah pembaca menafsirkan ulang Lilith sebagai lambang kebebasan perempuan.
long_description.en: Talmudic material also connects Lilith with darkness and sexuality. The Zohar later portrays her as wife of Adam and Satan in a mystical reading. In modern reinterpretations, some readers have made Lilith a symbol of women's freedom.

description.id: Alphabet of Ben Sira mengisahkan Lilith mengucapkan nama ilahi lalu terbang dan melarikan diri.
description.en: The Alphabet of Ben Sira has Lilith speak the divine name, fly, and flee.

note.id: Dalam Alphabet of Ben Sira, Lilith digambarkan sebagai istri awal Adam.
note.en: In the Alphabet of Ben Sira, Lilith is depicted as Adam's early wife.

short_description.id: Yūrei adalah roh orang meninggal dalam tradisi Jepang yang dapat tetap berada di dunia manusia.
short_description.en: Yūrei are spirits of deceased people in Japanese tradition that may remain in the human world.

long_description.id: Yūrei merujuk kepada roh orang yang telah meninggal. Sebagian kisah menggambarkan roh itu belum menyeberang ke alam lain karena alasan pribadi atau karena upacara pemakaman yang dianggap kurang memadai. Dalam seni dan sastra, gambaran yang dikenal ialah perempuan berambut hitam panjang, berpakaian pemakaman, dengan tangan menggantung dan tanpa kaki.
long_description.en: Yūrei refers to the spirits of deceased people. Some accounts describe them as remaining in the human world for personal reasons or because funeral rites were considered insufficient. In art and literature, a familiar image is a long-haired woman in burial clothes, with dangling hands and no feet.

long_description.id: Makna istilah ini berubah dalam sejarah Jepang. Pada masa kuno dan pertengahan yūrei lazim berarti jiwa orang mati dan belum dipandang dapat mengutuk. Sekitar abad kelima belas, istilah itu mulai dikaitkan dengan roh yang menyimpan dendam. Pada zaman Edo, cerita hantu, kabuki, dan seni cetak turut menampilkan sosok yūrei yang menakutkan.
long_description.en: The term changed meaning through Japanese history. In ancient and medieval usage yūrei usually meant the souls of the dead and were not thought able to curse. Around the fifteenth century the word began to describe resentful spirits. In the Edo period, ghost tales, kabuki, and prints helped present frightening yūrei.

long_description.id: Yūrei (幽霊) adalah figur dalam cerita rakyat Jepang, yang sepadan dengan hantu. Istilah tersebut terdiri dari dua huruf kanji, 幽 (yū), berarti "redup" atau "samar", dan 霊 (rei), berarti "jiwa" atau "spirit." Nama alternatifnya antara lain Bōrei (亡霊) yang berarti arwah orang meninggal, Shiryō (死霊) berarti jiwa orang mati, atau dalam pengertian yang lebih luas meliputi Yōkai (妖怪) atau Obake (お化け). Seperti padanan mereka dalam mitologi Tionghoa dan Barat, mereka diyakini sebagai jiwa setelah mati.
long_description.en: Yūrei (幽霊) are figures in Japanese folklore analogous to the Western concept of ghosts. The name consists of two kanji, 幽 (yū), meaning "faint" or "dim" and 霊 (rei), meaning "soul" or "spirit". Alternative names include Bōrei (亡霊), meaning ruined or departed spirit, Shiryō (死霊), meaning dead spirit, or the more encompassing Yōkai (妖怪) or Obake (お化け). Like their Western counterparts, they are thought to be spirits barred from a peaceful afterlife.

short_description.id: Onryō adalah roh pendendam dalam tradisi Jepang yang dipercaya dapat menimbulkan kutukan dan bencana.
short_description.en: Onryō are resentful spirits in traditions of Japan believed to cause curses and calamities.

long_description.id: Dalam kepercayaan Jepang kuno, onryō merujuk kepada arwah orang yang meninggal dengan rasa dendam dan dikhawatirkan dapat mengutuk. Roh seperti itu juga ditakuti sebagai penyebab wabah atau bencana besar. Orang berusaha menenangkan dan memuliakan mereka melalui upacara; praktik semacam ini meluas terutama pada masa Heian.
long_description.en: In ancient Japan, onryō are spirits of people who died with resentment and were feared as able to cast curses. Such spirits were also feared as causes of epidemics or major calamities. People sought to pacify and honor them through rites; such practices spread particularly in the Heian period.

long_description.id: Kisah Sugawara no Michizane menunjukkan satu contoh. Ia meninggal dalam pengasingan; setelah itu, bencana dan wabah dalam legenda dikaitkan dengan arwahnya. Ia diberi pengampunan dan kenaikan pangkat setelah wafat untuk menenangkannya, tetapi bencana dikisahkan berlanjut. Pada akhirnya ia didewakan sebagai Tenjin. Kisah ini menunjukkan bahwa roh yang ditakuti juga dapat menjadi objek pemujaan.
long_description.en: The story of Sugawara no Michizane gives an example. He died in exile, and later disasters and plagues were linked to his spirit in legend. He was pardoned and promoted after death in an attempt to appease him, but the calamities were said to continue. He was eventually deified as Tenjin. The account shows how a feared spirit could also become an object of worship.

long_description.id: Onryō (怨霊) atau hantu penasaran, adalah makhluk gaib dalam haha yang memiliki kemampuan untuk muncul di alam hayat/dunia manusia untuk membalas dendam. Dalam legenda dan cerita rakyat, kebanyakan onryō merupakan arwah wanita, tetapi onryō pria juga pernah disebutkan, khususnya dalam pementasan kabuki. Menurut legenda, onryō merupakan perwujudan arwah manusia yang saat masih hidup dilanda masalah dan berujung pada kematian mereka. Masalahnya meliputi persaingan, politik, atau penderitaan karena perubahan tingkah kekasih mereka. Setelah meninggal, arwah mereka menjadi hantu penasaran. Dunia arwah menurut kepercayaan Jepang terdiri dari tiga lapisan: surga (高天原, Takama ga hara), alam hayat atau alam kehidupan (葦原の中つ国, Ashihara no nakatsukuni), dan alam maut atau alam kematian (黄泉の国, Yomi no kumi). Tidak peduli siapa pun orangnya, setelah meninggal maka arwahnya akan pergi ke Yomi, bahkan bagi para Kami (dewa) sekalipun. Meskipun menurut mitologi Jepang jiwa yang sudah berada di alam maut tak dapat kembali lagi ke alam hayat, tetapi jiwa yang kuat dapat memengaruhi alam hayat entah berdasarkan niat yang baik maupun buruk. Dalam Kojiki (711-2) (kitab tertua tentang sejarah Jepang yang dimulai dari mitos penciptaannya) diceritakan bahwa ketika dewi Izanami wafat, dia mampu memberi kutukan dari Yomi ke alam hayat. Dalam arti yang sama, onryō mengacu pada arwah—khususnya manusia—yang berubah karena emosi luar biasa untuk melakukan kejahatan tersebut.
long_description.en: In Japanese traditional beliefs and literature, onryō (怨霊, lit. 'vengeful spirit', sometimes rendered "wrathful spirits", "hatred spirits", "resentful spirits", "ruthless spirits", "envious spirits", "dark spirits", "fallen spirits", or "downcast spirits") are a type of ghost (yūrei) believed to be capable of causing harm in the world of the living, injuring or killing enemies, or even causing natural disasters to exact vengeance to "redress" the wrongs they received while alive, then taking their spirits from their dying bodies. Onryō are often depicted as wronged women, who are traumatized, envious, disappointed, bitter, or just infuriated by what happened during life and exact revenge in death. These kinds of ghosts appear extremely vengeful, cruel, deranged, egotistical, bloodthirsty, and heartless. Emperor Sutoku, Taira no Masakado, and Sugawara no Michizane are called the Three Great Onryō of Japan (日本三大怨霊, Nihon Sandai Onryō) because they are considered to be the most powerful and revered onryō in Japanese history. After they died with resentment and anger, there was a series of deaths of political opponents, natural disasters, and wars, and the rulers enshrined them as kami and deified them in Shinto shrines to appease the resentment and anger that had turned them into onryō. Onryō are used as subjects in various traditional Japanese performing arts such as Noh, Kabuki, and Rakugo; For example, hannya is a Noh mask representing a female onryō. The reverence for onryō has been passed down to the present day. The head mound of Taira no Masakado (将門塚, Masakado-zuka or Shōmon-zuka), located between skyscrapers near Tokyo Station, was to be moved several times as part of urban redevelopment projects, but each move resulted in the death of a construction worker and a series of accidents. Although the buildings surrounding the Taira no Masakado mound have been rebuilt many times, the mound has remained intact between the high-rise buildings. Even today, the mound is carefully maintained. The term goryō (御霊) is often used as a synonym for onryō, but the term goryō is more commonly used to refer to the onryō that have become the object of the people's reverence after a noble person has died a politically unjust death. Goryō Shinko (御霊信仰) refers to the belief that the onryō of people who have died unfortunate deaths cause hauntings and disasters, and the belief that they are enshrined as kami to appease them.

short_description.id: Shikigami adalah roh pendamping dalam tradisi Onmyōdō yang kisah-kisahnya menampilkan beragam rupa dan tugas.
short_description.en: Shikigami are familiar spirits in Onmyōdō whose stories give them varied forms and tasks.

long_description.id: Shikigami disebut sebagai kami atau roh pendamping yang dipanggil dalam tradisi Onmyōdō. Nama lain yang tercatat ialah shikijin dan shiki no kami. Kisah-kisah menggambarkan mereka sebagai anak, lelaki muda, hewan kecil, atau setan; dalam banyak kisah wujudnya justru tidak terlihat. Dalam Konjaku monogatari, praktisi onmyōji menggunakan shikigami untuk sihir, ramalan, serta perintah sehari-hari.
long_description.en: Shikigami are described as kami or familiar spirits invoked in Onmyōdō. Recorded alternative names include shikijin and shiki no kami. Stories portray them as children, young men, small animals, or demons; in many accounts their form remains unseen. Konjaku monogatari says onmyōji practitioners summon them for magic, divination, and everyday commands.

long_description.id: Asal konsepnya diperdebatkan. Sebuah ensiklopedia menghubungkannya dengan dua belas dewa pelindung bulanan pada papan ramalan shikiban dan dengan hewan-hewan yang terkait pembagian waktu. Sebuah kajian menunjukkan bahwa para sarjana juga menafsirkan shikigami sebagai lambang metode ramalan, kutukan, ataupun makhluk gaib. Karena itu, gambaran roh pembantu adalah salah satu cara memahami tokoh ini, bukan definisi tunggal yang diterima semua sumber. Perbedaan penuturan dalam sastra klasik turut menjelaskan mengapa rupanya begitu beragam.
long_description.en: The concept’s origins are debated. An encyclopedia links it to twelve monthly tutelary deities on a shikiban divination board and to animals associated with the hours. A study shows that scholars have interpreted shikigami as a metaphor for divination, a curse, or a supernatural being. The familiar-spirit account is therefore one interpretation, not a settled definition. Variations in classical narratives help explain their many forms.

long_description.id: Shikigami (式神, juga dieja dengan Shiki-no-kami, 式の神) adalah sosok Kami yang berasal dari arwah manusia atau binatang yang meninggal dengan membawa perasaan dendam dan kebencian yang teramat sangat mendalam bersama-sama menuju ke alam kematiannya. Ajaran tentang praktik pemanggilan dan penyegelan Shikigami berasal dari ajaran Onmyōdō.
long_description.en: Shikigami (式神) (also read as Shiki-no-kami (式の神)) is the term for a being from Japanese folklore. According to the Shinto scholar Inoue Nobutaka, it is thought to be some sort of kami, represented by a small ghost. The belief of shikigami originates from Onmyōdō. According to the tradition of Onmyōdō, shikigami is a symbol of onmyōji's power because onmyōji can freely use shikigami with magical powers. It has been associated with "curses" since the 1000s of the Heian period, and was often depicted as a bird or a child in Japanese literature and Emakimono.

short_description.id: Ikiryō adalah roh orang yang masih hidup yang dalam kisah dapat meninggalkan tubuh dan mendatangi orang lain.
short_description.en: Ikiryō is the spirit of a living person that can leave the body and visit another person in stories.

long_description.id: Ikiryō, atau roh hidup, berangkat dari kepercayaan bahwa jiwa seseorang dapat keluar dari tubuhnya, mengganggu orang lain, lalu kembali. Sebuah kajian sastra membahas dua contohnya: Lady Rokujō dalam Genji monogatari dan seorang bangsawan perempuan tanpa nama dalam Konjaku monogatarishū. Dalam kedua kisah, penderitaan akibat hubungan cinta memicu perjalanan jiwa. Kajian itu membedakan Rokujō yang tidak menyadari perjalanannya dari tokoh Konjaku yang sengaja mengirim jiwanya untuk membalas dendam.
long_description.en: Ikiryō, or a living spirit, arises from a belief that a person’s soul can leave the body, trouble someone else, and return. A literary study compares Lady Rokujō in Genji monogatari with an unnamed noblewoman in Konjaku monogatarishū. In both stories, hurt tied to love motivates the soul’s journey. The study contrasts Rokujō, unaware of her spirit’s travels, with the Konjaku woman, who sends hers deliberately for revenge.

long_description.id: Pementasan Aoi no Ue mengolah kisah Rokujō: rohnya datang karena cemburu kepada Lady Aoi dan membuatnya sakit. Dalam pertunjukan itu, rasa cemburu menjelma sosok perempuan menyerupai setan, sebelum doa membawanya menuju ketenangan. Karena kisah-kisahnya berbeda dalam kesadaran tokoh dan akibatnya, ikiryō lebih tepat dipahami sebagai motif roh hidup daripada watak tunggal yang selalu bertindak sama.
long_description.en: The play Aoi no Ue reworks Rokujō’s story: jealousy sends her spirit against Lady Aoi and makes her ill. In the play, jealousy takes the form of a female ogre before prayer brings the spirit peace. Because the stories differ in the person’s awareness and outcome, ikiryō is best understood here as a living-spirit motif rather than a single character with fixed behavior.

statement.en: Ikiryō was believed to be a living person’s soul that could leave, cause trouble, and return.

claims.quote: This paper analyses examples of such phenomenon depicted in two literary sources: Lady Rokujō from Murasaki Shikibu’s (978? 1016?) Genji monogatari (1008) and an unnamed noblewoman from Konjaku monogatarishū (1120).

statement.en: The study examines Lady Rokujō in Genji monogatari and an unnamed noblewoman in Konjaku monogatarishū.

claims.quote: In both instances emotions play great role in creating ikiryō.

statement.id: Emosi berperan besar dalam kedua kisah ikiryō.
statement.en: Emotions are central to both ikiryō stories.

claims.quote: Women’s souls separate from the body and serve punishment for sufferings caused by unfaithful men.

long_description.id: Ikiryo (bahasa Jepang: 生霊 atau いきりょう) adalah sejenis hantu dalam mitologi Jepang atau yokai yang diperoleh dari orang yang masih hidup. Orang yang masih hidup dan melepas rohnya ke pada objek lain dapat juga dikatakan ikiryo. Banyak cara ikiryo dapat terwujud dari tubuh seseorang: selama saat sakaratul maut, pingsan, keinginan besar untuk bertemu dengan seseorang, atau bahkan digunakan seorang onryo atau dukun untuk melakukan praktik santet. Jadi, ikiryo adalah pelepasan roh atau transfer roh dari tubuh seseorang, dan wujud hantu dari manusia yang masih hidup. Di barat hal ini dikenal dengan proyek astral.
long_description.en: Ikiryō (生霊; lit. 'living ghost'), also known as shōryō (しょうりょう), seirei (せいれい), or ikisudama (いきすだま), is a disembodied spirit or ghost in Japanese popular belief and fiction that leaves the body of a living person and subsequently haunts other people or places, sometimes across great distances. The term(s) are used in contrast to shiryō, which refers to the spirit of those who are already deceased.

short_description.id: Swan Maiden adalah tokoh perempuan gaib dalam pola cerita lintas budaya tentang jubah bulu yang memungkinkan ia pergi dari dunia manusia.
short_description.en: The Swan Maiden is a supernatural woman in cross-cultural stories about a feather robe that lets her leave the human world.

long_description.id: Swan Maiden adalah sebutan bagi pola cerita, bukan satu tokoh dengan riwayat tetap. Kajian folklor menyebut kisah ini tersebar di banyak budaya: seorang perempuan gaib dipaksa menikah dengan lelaki yang menahan benda kunci kebebasannya, lalu pergi ketika benda itu kembali. Dalam salah satu cerita yang dikumpulkan, tujuh perempuan berbaju bulu turun ke danau. Seorang pemburu mengambil jubah si bungsu, menyembunyikannya, dan membuatnya menikah. Ketika anak mereka menemukan jubah itu, perempuan tersebut mengenakannya dan terbang pergi.
long_description.en: Swan Maiden names a story pattern rather than one person with a fixed biography. A folklore study describes stories in many cultures in which a supernatural woman is forced to marry a man who holds the key to her freedom; she leaves when she regains it. In one collected tale, seven feather-robed women descend to a lake. A hunter hides the youngest woman’s robe and makes her marry him. When their child finds it, she puts it on and flies away.

long_description.id: Sebuah versi dari Jepang yang diterjemahkan dalam kumpulan cerita yang sama memakai perempuan kahyangan dan jubah bulu, tanpa menyebut ia berubah menjadi angsa. Seorang nelayan menemukan jubah itu; sang perempuan mengatakan ia tidak dapat kembali ke langit tanpanya. Nelayan akhirnya mengembalikan jubah setelah ia berjanji menari. Ia pun mengenakannya, menari di udara, lalu menghilang. Perbedaan itu menunjukkan bahwa bentuk burung dan akhir cerita bervariasi; unsur yang berulang adalah jubah yang menahan atau membebaskan perempuan gaib.
long_description.en: A Japanese version translated in the same collection features a heavenly maiden and a feather robe without saying she becomes a swan. A fisherman finds the robe; the maiden says she cannot return to heaven without it. He eventually gives it back in return for a dance. She puts it on, dances in the air, and disappears. Bird form and endings vary; the recurring element here is the robe that constrains or releases a supernatural woman.

long_description.en: The "swan maiden" (German: Schwanjungfrau) is a tale classified as ATU 400, "The Swan Maiden" or "The Man on a Quest for His Lost Wife", in which a man makes a pact with, or marries, a supernatural female being who later departs. The wife shapeshifts from human to bird form with the use of a feathered cloak (or otherwise turns into a beast by donning animal skin). The discussion is sometimes limited to cases in which the wife is specifically a swan, a goose, or at least some other kind of bird, as in Enzyklopädie des Märchens. The key to the transformation is usually a swan skin, or a garment with swan feathers attached. In the typical story, a maiden is (usually bathing) in some body of water, a man furtively steals, hides, or burns her feather garment (motif K 1335, D 361.1), which prevents her from flying away (or swimming away, etc.), forcing her to become his wife. She is often one of several maidens present (often celestial beings), and often it is the youngest who gets captured. The bird wife eventually leaves this husband in many cases. The oldest narrative example of this type is Chinese, recorded in the Sou shen ji ("In Search of the Supernatural", 4th century), etc. There are many analogues around the world, notably the Völundarkviða and Grimms' Fairy Tales KHM 193 "The Drummer". There are also many parallels involving creatures other than swans.

long_description.en: The "swan maiden" (German: Schwanjungfrau) is a tale classified as ATU 400, "The Swan Maiden" or "The Man on a Quest for His Lost Wife", in which a man makes a pact with, or marries, a supernatural female being who later departs. The wife shapeshifts from human to bird form with the use of a feathered cloak (or otherwise turns into a beast by donning animal skin). The discussion is sometimes limited to cases in which the wife is specifically a swan, a goose, or at least some other kind of bird, as in Enzyklopädie des Märchens. The key to the transformation is usually a swan skin, or a garment with swan feathers attached. In the typical story, a maiden is (usually bathing) in some body of water, a man furtively steals, hides, or burns her feather garment (motif K 1335, D 361.1), which prevents her from flying away (or swimming away, etc.), forcing her to become his wife. She is often one of several maidens present (often celestial beings), and often it is the youngest who gets captured. The bird wife eventually leaves this husband in many cases. The oldest narrative example of this type is Chinese, recorded in the Sou shen ji ("In Search of the Supernatural", 4th century), etc. There are many analogues around the world, notably the Völundarkviða and Grimms' Fairy Tales KHM 193 "The Drummer". There are also many parallels involving creatures other than swans.

short_description.id: Zashiki-warashi adalah roh rumah yang tampak seperti anak kecil dan dipercaya berkaitan dengan keberuntungan penghuninya.
short_description.en: Zashiki-warashi is a childlike house spirit believed to be connected with a household’s fortune.

long_description.id: Dalam cerita Tōno di wilayah Iwate, zashiki-warashi digambarkan sebagai dewa rumah yang tampak seperti anak. Versi lain menyebutnya roh anak yang tinggal di kamar atau gudang. Kehadirannya dipercaya membuat rumah makmur, sedangkan kepergiannya dianggap tanda keluarga akan miskin. Pemandu wisata Iwate menggambarkannya sebagai roh pelindung rumah berwujud anak laki-laki, sehingga sebutan “roh” dan “dewa rumah” sama-sama muncul dalam penuturan tentangnya.
long_description.en: In stories from Tōno in Iwate, zashiki-warashi is described as a household deity looking like a child. Another account calls it a child spirit living in rooms or storehouses. Its presence is believed to bring prosperity, while its departure foretells poverty. An Iwate guide calls it a boy-shaped guardian spirit of the house, showing that both spirit and household deity are used for this figure.

long_description.id: Folkloris Yanagita Kunio menerbitkan kumpulan cerita Tōno pada 1910, membantu melestarikan kisah daerah itu. Sebuah penginapan menceritakan bahwa zashiki-warashi tinggal di ruang belakang dan orang yang melihatnya akan berhasil dalam hidup. Kisah tersebut tetap dipakai sebagai bagian dari identitas tempat wisata setempat. Laporan penampakan yang disebut dalam bahan wisata merupakan kesaksian tentang kepercayaan, bukan bukti keberadaan makhluk itu.
long_description.en: Folklorist Yanagita Kunio published a Tōno story collection in 1910, preserving local tales. An inn tells visitors that zashiki-warashi lives in a back room and that seeing it brings success. The story remains part of local tourism. Sightings mentioned in tourist materials are reports about belief, not proof that the being exists.

long_description.id: Zashiki warashi (座敷童子) adalah arwah anak-anak yang terutama dipercaya penduduk Prefektur Iwate, Jepang. Arwah ini dipercaya sebagai kami (dewa), yang tinggal di zashiki atau gudang; warashi berarti anak-anak. Menurut cerita rakyat Jepang, zashiki warashi mendatangkan kekayaan untuk rumah yang ditinggalinya. Meskipun ia suka mengusili anggota keluarga yang tinggal di rumah itu, tetapi akan mendatangkan keberuntungan kepada anggota keluarga yang dapat melihatnya. Cerita zashiki warashi menjadi populer setelah Kunio Yanagita menerbitkan kumpulan cerita legenda Tōno Monogatari (Hikayat dari Tōno) dan Ishigami Mondō (Tanya Jawab mengenai Ishigami). Salah satu kamar di penginapan Ryokufoso yang berada di Ninohe, Prefektur Iwate dipercaya ditinggali oleh zashiki warashi. Penginapan ini telah berulang kali dijadikan bahan liputan media massa, termasuk acara televisi di Jepang.
long_description.en: Zashiki-warashi (座敷童子; or 座敷童, "parlor child"), sometimes also called zashiki bokko (座敷ぼっこ; "parlor boyo"), are spirit-like beings told about mostly in the Iwate Prefecture. They are said to be yokai that live in parlors or storage rooms, and that they perform pranks. It is believed that people who saw one would receive good fortune. There are also legends of how they would bring fortune to families. They are also known from Kunio Yanagita's Tōno Monogatari, Ishigami Mondō, and stories about them appear in the 17th and 18th chapters of the Tōno Monogatari and the 87th chapter titled "Zashiki-warashi" of the Tōno Monogatari Shūi. In the 17th chapter, it is written "families with whom this spirit dwells become prosperous" (kono kami no yadoritamafu ihe ha fūki jizai nari to ifu koto nari).

short_description.id: Toyotama-hime adalah dewi laut, istri Hoori dan ibu Ugayafukiaezu.
short_description.en: Toyotama-hime is a sea-linked goddess, the wife of Hoori and mother of Ugayafukiaezu.

long_description.id: Toyotama-hime adalah putri dewa laut Watatsumi. Ia bertemu Hoori, yang juga disebut Hohodemi, di istana bawah laut, lalu menjadi istrinya. Setelah hidup bersama di sana selama tiga tahun, Hoori kembali ke daratan. Toyotama-hime menyusul untuk melahirkan putra mereka, Ugayafukiaezu, dan meminta pondok bersalin beratap bulu burung pecuk. Kisah perkawinan dan kelahirannya tercatat dalam Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki.
long_description.en: Toyotama-hime is the daughter of the sea deity Watatsumi. She meets Hoori, also called Hohodemi, in the undersea palace and becomes his wife. After three years together there, Hoori returns to land. She follows to give birth to their son Ugayafukiaezu and asks for a birthing hut roofed with cormorant feathers. Her marriage and motherhood appear in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.

long_description.id: Saat bersalin, Toyotama-hime meminta suaminya tidak melihat ke dalam pondok. Ia melanggar larangan itu dan melihat wujud aslinya, lalu Toyotama-hime kembali ke laut karena malu. Dalam penjelasan Kojiki, wujudnya adalah wani, yang oleh peneliti kerap dipahami sebagai hiu besar; teks utama Nihon Shoki menyebut naga. Karena sumber lama berbeda, menyebutnya hanya sebagai naga akan menghilangkan variasi kisah. Pemujaan setempat masih berlangsung: di kuilnya orang berdoa untuk kesehatan dan kulit yang indah.
long_description.en: During childbirth, Toyotama-hime asks her husband not to look inside the hut. He breaks the taboo, sees her transformed form, and she returns to the sea in shame. The Kojiki calls the form wani, often understood by scholars as a great shark; the main Nihon Shoki text says dragon. Calling her simply a dragon would lose this variation. Local worship continues: at her shrine people pray for health and beautiful skin.

Ia adalah putri cantik dari Ryūjin, dewa laut. Ia menikahi sebuah pemburu yang bernama Hoori dan melahirkan seorang putra, yang kemudian menghasilkan Kaisar Jimmu, Kaisar Jepang pertama.
long_description.en: Toyotama-hime (Japanese: 豊玉姫) is a goddess in Japanese mythology who appears in Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. She is the daughter of the sea deity, Watatsumi, and the wife of Hoori. She is known as the paternal grandmother of Emperor Jimmu, the first emperor of Japan. Toyotama marries the prince Hoori, but returns to the sea when he breaks the vow not to spy on her while she goes through childbirth. The child she gave birth to was Ugayafukiaezu.

short_description.id: Ameonna adalah sosok “perempuan hujan” dalam gambar yōkai Sekien yang berkaitan dengan kisah dewi awan dan hujan.
short_description.en: Ameonna is a “rain woman” in Sekien’s yōkai art, linked to a tale of a cloud-and-rain goddess.

long_description.id: Ameonna berarti “perempuan hujan”. Dalam Konjaku Hyakki Shūi, Toriyama Sekien menggambarkannya berdiri di bawah hujan sambil menjilat tangannya. Keterangan yang menyertai gambar merujuk kisah perempuan ilahi Gunung Wu yang berubah menjadi awan pada pagi hari dan hujan pada petang hari. Sekien mengajukan perbandingan dengan sosok itu, bukan uraian tentang riwayat hidup atau kekuatan tetap ameonna.
long_description.en: Ameonna means “rain woman.” In Konjaku Hyakki Shūi, Toriyama Sekien portrays her standing in rain and licking her hand. The caption refers to a divine woman of Mount Wu who becomes a cloud in the morning and rain in the evening. Sekien suggests a resemblance, rather than giving a life story or fixed list of powers for ameonna.

long_description.id: Kisah awan pagi dan hujan petang berasal dari cerita dalam puisi Gaotang Fu yang dikaitkan dengan Song Yu. Penggunaan modern kata ameonna juga dapat berarti seseorang yang dianggap selalu membawa hujan ke acara penting; ini adalah sebutan bagi manusia, bukan kemunculan makhluk pada gambar Sekien. Ada pula kisah tentang perempuan di wilayah Shimoina yang disebut Ameonba dan muncul pada malam hujan. Nama serta cerita setempat itu perlu dibedakan dari gambar Sekien.
long_description.en: The morning-cloud and evening-rain allusion comes from the Gaotang Fu associated with Song Yu. In modern usage, ameonna can also describe a person said to bring rain to important occasions; that is a label for a person, rather than an apparition in Sekien’s picture. Another account names a woman called Ameonba who appears on rainy nights in Shimoina. This local name and tale should be kept distinct from Sekien’s image.

sources.title: Ame-onna: Rain Woman’s Original Ghost Story
sources.author: Thersa Matsuura

long_description.id: Ame onna (bahasa Jepang Kanji: 雨女, Hiragana: あめおんな - wanita hujan) atau Ame onba adalah yokai dalam cerita rakyat Jepang. Ia sering muncul ketika hujan turun pada siang atau malam hari, terutama di jalanan dan gang-gang yang gelap. Konon ia dapat mendatangkan hujan kemanapun ia pergi. Penggambarannya seperti wanita jahat dengan wajah yang jelek, pakaian basah kuyup, dan sering menjilati air hujan di tangannya sendiri. Asal ame onna berakar dari kepercayaan masyarakat kuno di Jepang dan Tiongkok yang meyakini adanya dewa pembawa hujan. Ame onna erat kaitannya denga dewa hujan rintik, tetapi ia berperilaku jahat. Menurut legenda, bersama dengan turunnya hujan rintik, ia akan berkeliaran di desa-desa kecil dan mencari bayi yang baru lahir untuk dibawanya ke dunia lain.
long_description.en: Ameonna (雨(あめ)女(おんな), "rain woman") is a Japanese yōkai thought to call forth rain, illustrated in Toriyama Sekien's Konjaku Hyakki Shūi as a woman standing in the rain and licking her hand. In modern usage in Japan, "ameonna" (or the male equivalent "ameotoko") refers to an unlucky person that seems to be jinxed to have the rain follow them wherever they may go, thus gaining a reputation for ruining special events such as weddings or sporting events.

long_description.id: Dōsojin (道祖神, "dewa pelindung jalan") adalah nama yang umum bagi sejenis kami yang populer dipuja di wilayah Kantō dan area di sekitarnya. Sebagai dewa pelindung perbatasan, umat Shinto percaya bahwa mereka melindungi para pelancong dan penduduk dari wabah penyakit dan gangguan roh jahat. Mereka juga disebut Sae no kami atau Sai no kami (障の神・塞の神), Dōrokujin (道陸神) atau Shakujin (石神, "dewa batu"). Sering kali dilambangkan sebagai manusia berpasangan, tetapi dibuat patungnya dalam wujud alat kelamin pria dan wanita, dalam bentuk batu besar atau patung, atau bahkan pilar tinggi di sepanjang jalan. Kadang kala dōsojin dikuilkan di sebuah kuil kecil di pinggir jalan yang disebut hokora. Dalam bentuk seperti falus, mereka dihubungkan dengan kelahiran dan penciptaan, dan oleh karena itu sebagai harmoni perkawinan.
long_description.en: Dōsojin (道祖神) are a class of protective Shinto deities (kami) commonly venerated in eastern Japan, particularly in the Kantō, Chūbu, and Tōhoku regions. They are associated with liminal spaces such as village boundaries, crossroads, and mountain passes, and are believed to ward off evil spirits, epidemics, and other harmful influences that threaten individuals or communities during transitional stages of life.2 Dōsojin (道祖神; literally, "road ancestor deity") is a generic name for a type of Shinto kami popularly worshipped in Kantō and neighboring areas in Japan where, as tutelary deities of borders and paths, they are believed to protect travellers, pilgrims, villages, and individuals in "transitional stages" from epidemics and evil spirits. Also called Sae no kami or Sai no kami (障の神・塞の神), Dōrokujin (道陸神) or Shakujin (石神; literally: "stone kami"). Dōsojin are often represented as a human couple, carved male or female genitals, large stones or statues, or even tall poles along a road. Dōsojin are sometimes housed in small roadside Shinto shrines called hokora. In rural areas Dōsojin can be found at village boundaries, in mountain passes, or along byways, and in urban areas they can be seen at street corners or near bridges. When shaped like a phallus, they are associated with birth, procreation, and marital harmony. When represented as a human couple, Dōsojin are revered as deities of boundaries, roads, travellers, villagers, marriage, fertility, health, agriculture, harvest, procreation, guardianship, defense and protection. They were used as protective markers in village boundaries as fertility symbols for the ensure of the growth of crops.

long_description.en: Oshiroibabā (Japanese: 白粉ばばあ; lit. "oshiroi (white facial powder) old woman") or Oshiroibabā-san (白粉ばあさん) is a yōkai old woman from the Totsukawa river in Yoshino District, Nara Prefecture. The oshiroibabā is said to be a yōkai in the form of an old woman who appears while dragging a mirror and making a jingling sound. Toriyama Sekien's Konjaku Hyakki Shūi depicts an old woman with a very bent back, wearing a large broken umbrella on her head, holding a walking stick with her right hand and a tokkuri (flask for sake) in her left hand, under the name of oshiroibabā. The commentary on the picture says, “the goddess of red and white oshiroi (facial powder) powder is called Shifunsenjo, and oshiroibabā must be an attendant of this goddess,” but it is unclear whether this is supposed to be the same oshiroibabā in Nara folklore. She is said to have applied this white powder all over her face, but this application is so thick and messy that just looking at her is said to be terrifying. Folklorist Morihiko Fujisawa's book "Zusetsu Minzoku Zenshū" (図説民俗学全集) purports that they are the same kind of yokai as yuki-onna, and to appear on snowy nights in the Noto region of Ishikawa Prefecture in search of sake, but the actual existence of such a tradition has not been confirmed in Noto, and it has been noted that Fujisawa may have invented this in consideration of the Konjaku Hyakki Shūi. It has also been suggested that there may be some relation between the oshiroibabā, and the mountain yōkai, the yama-uba and yama-hime, given that both of these have stories about begging travelers for white facial powder (oshiroi) and to have appeared at the foot of mountains to buy sake.

short_description.id: Leanan sídhe ("kekasih peri") adalah sosok mitologi Kelt, perempuan cantik dari Aos Sí yang mengambil kekasih manusia; para kekasihnya hidup singkat tetapi penuh ilham.
short_description.en: The leanan sídhe ('fairy lover') is a figure of Celtic myth, a beautiful woman of the Aos Sí who takes a human lover; her lovers live brief but inspired lives.

long_description.id: Leannán sídhe (Irlandia/Irish, harfiah "kekasih peri"; Gaelik Skotlandia/Scottish Gaelic: leannan sìth; Manx: lhiannan shee) adalah sosok dari mitologi Kelt (Celtic). Ia digambarkan sebagai perempuan cantik dari Aos Sí ("orang gundukan peri") yang mengambil kekasih manusia, dan para kekasihnya dikatakan hidup singkat tetapi sangat terilhami. Namanya berasal dari kata Gaelik untuk kekasih dan sebutan bagi penghuni gundukan peri. Meski biasanya berwujud peri perempuan, ada setidaknya satu rujukan tentang leannán sídhe laki-laki yang mengganggu perempuan fana.
long_description.en: The leannán sídhe (Irish, literally 'fairy lover'; Scottish Gaelic leannan sìth; Manx lhiannan shee) comes from Celtic myth. She is shown as a lovely woman of the Aos Sí ('people of the fairy mounds') who chooses a human lover, and those lovers are said to live short but deeply inspired lives. The name joins Gaelic words for sweetheart and for the dwellers of fairy mounds. Though usually a female fairy, there is at least one account of a male leannán sídhe troubling a mortal woman.

long_description.id: Sebuah versi mitos ini dipopulerkan selama Kebangkitan Kelt (Celtic Revival) akhir abad kesembilan belas; Jane Wilde ("Speranza") menyebutnya dalam Ancient Legends, Mystic Charms and Superstitions of Ireland (1887). W. B. Yeats mempopulerkan versinya sendiri yang menonjolkan sifat hampir vampiriknya: ia muse cantik yang memberi ilham kepada seniman sebagai ganti cinta dan pengabdian, tetapi hubungan gaib itu berujung kegilaan dan kematian. Menurut artikel de, sosok serupa Lhiannan Shee dikenal di Isle of Man, dan para peri ini menghabiskan nyawa kekasihnya serta tak membiarkan mereka lolos bahkan setelah mati.
long_description.en: A version of the myth spread during the Celtic Revival of the late nineteenth century; Jane Wilde ('Speranza') mentions it in her Ancient Legends, Mystic Charms and Superstitions of Ireland (1887). W. B. Yeats popularised his own take stressing her near-vampiric side: a beautiful muse giving an artist inspiration in return for love and devotion, an affair that ends in madness and death. According to the de article a similar Lhiannan Shee is known on the Isle of Man, and these fairies use up their lovers' lives and let them go not even in death.

did_you_know.id: Menurut W. B. Yeats, penyair Gaelik mati muda karena leanan sídhe gelisah dan tak membiarkan mereka lama di bumi.
did_you_know.en: According to W. B. Yeats, Gaelic poets die young because the leanan sídhe is restless and will not let them stay long on earth.

long_description.en: The leannán sídhe (Irish: [ˈl̠ʲan̪ˠaːnˠ ˈʃiː]; lit. 'fairy lover'; Scottish Gaelic: leannan sìth, Manx: lhiannan shee) is a figure from Celtic mythology. She is depicted as a beautiful woman of the Aos Sí ("people of the fairy mounds") who takes a human lover. Lovers of the leannán sídhe are said to live brief, though highly inspired, lives. The name comes from the Gaelic words for a sweetheart or lover and the term for inhabitants of fairy mounds (fairy). While the leannán sídhe is most often depicted as a female fairy, there is at least one reference to a male leannán sídhe troubling a mortal woman. A version of the myth was popularized during the Celtic Revival in the late 19th-century. The leannán sídhe is mentioned by Jane Wilde, writing as "Speranza", in her 1887 Ancient Legends, Mystic Charms and Superstitions of Ireland. W. B. Yeats popularized his own 'newly-ancient' version of the leannán sídhe, emphasizing the spirit's almost vampiric tendencies. As he imagined it, the leannán sídhe is depicted as a beautiful muse who offers inspiration to an artist in exchange for their love and devotion; although the supernatural affair leads to madness and eventual death for the artist: The Leanhaun Shee (fairy mistress) seeks the love of mortals. If they refuse, she must be their slave; if they consent, they are hers, and can only escape by finding another to take their place. The fairy lives on their life, and they waste away. Death is no escape from her. She is the Gaelic muse, for she gives inspiration to those she persecutes. The Gaelic poets die young, for she is restless, and will not let them remain long on earth—this malignant phantom.

short_description.id: Far darrig (fear dearg, "Lelaki Merah") adalah peri dalam mitologi Irlandia yang mengenakan mantel dan topi merah dan gemar bercanda keji.
short_description.en: The far darrig (fear dearg, 'Red Man') is a fairy of Irish myth who wears a red coat and cap and loves gruesome practical jokes.

long_description.id: Far darrig atau fear dearg adalah jenis peri dalam mitologi Irlandia (Irish). Nama far darrig adalah pelafalan Anglophone dari kata Irlandia fear dearg, "Lelaki Merah" (Red Man), karena ia dikatakan mengenakan mantel dan topi merah. Mereka kadang disebut Rat Boys karena konon gemuk, berkulit gelap berbulu, bermoncong panjang, dan berekor kurus. Far darrig umumnya digambarkan pendek, kadang tinggi, dan dikatakan dapat mengubah ukurannya; uraian T. Crofton Croker tahun 1832 dari Munster menyebut tingginya sekitar 2,5 kaki, berwajah keriput, berambut kelabu panjang, dan bertopi kerucut.
long_description.en: The far darrig or fear dearg is a kind of fairy in Irish myth. The name is an Anglophone rendering of the Irish fear dearg, 'Red Man', for the red coat and cap he is said to have on. They are sometimes called Rat Boys, being said to be fat, with dark hairy skin, long snouts and thin tails. Usually short though at times tall, the far darrig is said to change size; an 1832 account by T. Crofton Croker from Munster makes them about 2.5 feet tall, wrinkle-faced, long grey-haired and wearing a sugarloaf hat.

long_description.id: Dalam Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry yang disunting W. B. Yeats, far darrig digolongkan peri penyendiri bersama leprechaun dan clurichaun, dan disebut sibuk dengan lelucon, terutama lelucon keji, misalnya menukar bayi dengan changeling. Menolak permintaan far darrig membawa sial karena mereka sangat kreatif dalam memikirkan hukuman. Menurut artikel fr, ia cenderung memaksa penghuni rumah menerimanya dan memberinya tempat terbaik di dekat perapian, lalu mengeringkan pakaiannya yang busuk di atas tungku; jika ditolak, ia akan terus mengganggu mereka.
long_description.en: In Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry, edited by W. B. Yeats, the far darrig is classed as a solitary fairy with the leprechaun and clurichaun, and is said to busy himself with practical jokes, above all gruesome ones, such as swapping babies for changelings. Refusing a far darrig's request was unlucky, as they were very inventive with punishments. According to the fr article he tends to force householders to take him in and give him the best seat by the fire, then dries his foul clothes over the hearth; if refused, he plagues them without end.

long_description.en: A far darrig or fear dearg is a faerie type in Irish mythology. The name far darrig is an Anglophone pronunciation of the Irish words fear dearg, meaning Red Man, as the far darrig is said to wear a red coat and cap. They are sometimes known as Rat Boys as they are said to be rather fat, have dark, hairy skin, long snouts and skinny tails. The far derrig is generally described as short, while sometimes described as tall. It's said the far derrig has the ability to change sizes. An 1832 description from T. Crofton Croaker in Munster says the far derrig are around 2.5 feet tall with a wrinkled face, long grey hair, and a sugarloaf hat. According to Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry, the far darrig is classified as a solitary fairy along with the leprechaun and the clurichaun, all of whom are "most sluttish, slouching, jeering, mischievous phantoms". The far darrig in particular is described as one who "busies himself with practical joking, especially with gruesome joking". One example of this is replacing babies with changelings. They are also said to have some connection to nightmares. Refusing any request from a far derrig was unlucky, as they were very imaginative in thinking of punishments. When not playing jokes, the far darrig spend much of their time smoking by campfires and thinking. They will eat a meal if offered, and the presence of one in a house is said to bring good luck.

long_description.en: A kumbhāṇḍa (Sanskrit) or kumbhaṇḍa (Pāli) is one of a group of dwarfish, misshapen spirits among the lesser deities of Buddhist mythology. Kumbhāṇḍa was a dialectal form for "gourd", so they may get their name from being thought to resemble gourds in some way, e.g. in having big stomachs. But kumbhāṇḍa can also be interpreted as "pot-egg"; since "egg" (aṇḍa) was a common euphemism for "testicle", the kumbhāṇḍas were imagined having testicles "as big as pots". The terms kumbhāṇḍa and yakṣa are sometimes used for the same creature; yakṣa in these cases is the more general term, including a variety of lower deities. The kumbhāṇḍas are classed among the Cāturmahārājika deities, and are subject to the Great King Virūḍhaka, Guardian of the South. One of their chiefs is called Kumbhīra. According to the Dà zhìdù lùn, greedy officers are reborn as kumbhāṇḍhas.

long_description.en: Naale Baa (Kannada: ನಾಳೆ ಬಾ, romanized: Nāḷe Bā [n̪aːɭe baː]; lit. 'Come Tomorrow') is a popular folk legend which features prominently in areas across Karnataka, India. "Naale Baa" has been found written on the doors and walls of the towns and villages for certain years. People write this on walls to prevent the entry of a malevolent spirit into their homes. It is believed that a malevolent spirit or witch roams around at night to take children away. In some variations, people believed that a demon roams around, knocks on doors and calls out names of people imitating the voice of their kin. If the person replies, they are said to die vomiting blood or by heart failure. There are also variations of the story where the spirit is believed to be a female ghost in search of her husband. She is known to take away the man of the house, often target those between 20 to 50 years of age, who is often the sole earning member of the family, thereby bringing bad luck to the entire household. Naale Baa went viral during the 1990s in Karnataka specially in rural Bangalore, gaining widespread popularity from the areas of Malleswaram and Rajajinagar which were considered sub-urban Bangalore at that time. The residents came up with the smart idea of writing "Naale Baa" outside the doors and the walls of their houses. It was believed that when the ghost read this sign, it goes back to come again the next day, only for the cycle to keep repeating. Practically, some claim it was a mass hysteria faced by young men living in those areas while some others claim that it was the behaviour of a sexually narcissistic women who might have targeted young men of that area. Every year, April 1 is also celebrated as Naale Baa day.

short_description.en: Abcán is the dwarf poet and musician of the Tuatha Dé Danann in Irish myth, owner of a bronze boat with a tin sail.

long_description.id: Dalam mitologi Irlandia (Irish), Abcán (ejaan modern: Abhcán) adalah penyair dan musisi kerdil Tuatha Dé Danann, dewa-dewa Kelt (Celtic) awal Irlandia (Ireland). Ia dikatakan memiliki perahu perunggu dengan layar timah. Menurut artikel es, ia pertama kali muncul dalam mitos Ruad dan disebut dewa mitologi Irlandia yang melayani Tuatha Dé Danann.
long_description.en: Irish myth makes Abcán, spelled Abhcán today, a dwarf who served as poet and musician to the Tuatha Dé Danann, Ireland's early Celtic gods. He was said to own a bronze boat with a tin sail. According to the es article he first appears in the myth of Ruad and is called a god of Irish myth serving the Tuatha Dé Danann.

long_description.id: Dalam kisah kematian dewi Ruad, Abcán adalah kerdil yang menyeberangkannya dari Dunia Lain ke dunia ini agar ia dapat merayu manusia bernama Aed Srónmár; suara nyanyian putri duyung, atau dalam sebagian versi musik dari gundukan peri, membuatnya melompat ke air dan tenggelam. Dalam kisah lain Abcán ditangkap pahlawan Cúchulainn, tetapi membebaskan diri dengan memainkan nina bobo yang begitu memikat hingga sang pejuang tertidur. Ia banyak kemiripannya, dan mungkin nama lain, dengan musisi kerdil Fer Í.
long_description.en: In the tale of the goddess Ruad's death, Abcán is the dwarf who ferries her from the Otherworld to this one so she can seduce a mortal, Aed Srónmár; the singing of mermaids, or in some versions music from a fairy mound, makes her leap into the water and drown. In another story the hero Cúchulainn captures Abcán, who frees himself by playing lullabies so irresistible that the warrior falls asleep. He closely resembles the dwarf musician Fer Í and may simply be the same figure under a different name.

short_description.id: Rübezahl adalah roh gunung dari cerita rakyat Jerman, Polandia, dan Ceko yang menguasai cuaca Pegunungan Raksasa dan bisa berganti rupa.
short_description.en: Rübezahl is a mountain spirit of German, Polish and Czech folklore who rules the weather of the Giant Mountains and can change his shape.

long_description.id: Rübezahl, dalam bahasa Polandia Liczyrzepa dan dalam bahasa Ceko Krakonoš, adalah roh gunung Pegunungan Raksasa di perbatasan Republik Ceko dan Polandia. Dalam legenda ia tampil sebagai raksasa, gnom, atau roh gunung yang suasana hatinya berubah-ubah: ramah kepada orang baik, mengajari mereka pengobatan dan memberi hadiah, tetapi membalas dengan keras siapa pun yang mengejeknya.
long_description.en: Rübezahl, Liczyrzepa in Polish and Krakonoš in Czech, is the mountain spirit of the Giant Mountains on the border between the Czech Republic and Poland. In legend he appears as a capricious giant, gnome or mountain spirit: friendly to good people, teaching them medicine and giving gifts, but taking severe revenge on anyone who mocks him.

long_description.id: Ia dianggap penguasa cuaca pegunungan yang tiba-tiba mengirim petir, kabut, hujan, dan salju walau matahari bersinar. Wujudnya beragam: biarawan berjubah kelabu, penambang, tukang, hewan, atau benda seperti tunggul pohon, batu, dan awan. Ia juga kadang menyesatkan pengembara dan memiliki kebun tanaman ajaib yang dijaganya.
long_description.en: He is held to be the weather lord of the mountains, sending sudden lightning, fog, rain and snow even in sunshine. His shapes vary: a monk in a grey habit, a miner, a craftsman, an animal, or objects such as a tree stump, a stone or a cloud. He also sometimes leads walkers astray and owns a garden of wondrous herbs that he defends.

long_description.id: Asal namanya tidak jelas. Johann Karl August Musäus mengisahkan Rübezahl menculik seorang putri yang memintanya menghitung lobak (Rüben) di ladang, lalu kabur selagi ia menghitung; tafsiran lain mengaitkannya dengan kata Jerman Hulu Pertengahan zagel, "ekor". "Rübezahl" adalah julukan ejekan yang membangkitkan amarahnya; sebutan hormatnya antara lain "Herr der Berge".
long_description.en: The origin of his name is unclear. Johann Karl August Musäus told how Rübezahl abducted a princess who asked him to count the turnips (Rüben) in a field and fled while he counted; another reading links it to Middle High German zagel, 'tail'. 'Rübezahl' is a mocking nickname that rouses his anger; respectful names include 'Herr der Berge'.

long_description.id: Dalam dongeng Ceko, Krakonoš dipandang sebagai penjaga Pegunungan Raksasa yang memberi orang ragi asam dan menciptakan sup kyselo; dari setan pembawa badai ia berkembang menjadi pelindung orang miskin di pegunungannya. Ia pertama kali digambarkan pada peta Martin Helwig tahun 1561, sedangkan kisahnya pertama dibukukan oleh Johannes Praetorius pada 1662.
long_description.en: In Czech tales Krakonoš is the guardian of the Giant Mountains who gave people sourdough and invented kyselo soup; from a storm-bringing demon he grew into a protector of the poor in his mountains. He was first depicted on a 1561 map by Martin Helwig, while his story was first written down by Johannes Praetorius in 1662.

literal_meaning.id: penghitung lobak (menurut kisah Musäus); kemungkinan juga dari zagel, "ekor"
literal_meaning.en: turnip counter (after Musäus's tale); possibly also from zagel, 'tail'

short_description.id: Hödekin, "Topi Kecil", adalah kobold atau roh rumah dalam cerita rakyat Jerman yang menghantui kastel Uskup Hildesheim; ia menolong tetapi membalas dendam dengan kejam bila dihina.
short_description.en: Hödekin, 'Little Hat', is a kobold or house spirit of German folklore who haunted the castle of the Bishop of Hildesheim; helpful, yet murderously vengeful when insulted.

long_description.id: Hödekin (juga Hödeken, Hütgin, Hüdekin, atau Hütchen) adalah kobold atau roh rumah dalam cerita rakyat Jerman. Namanya, bentuk kecil yang berarti "Topi Kecil", merujuk topi pileus yang dikenakannya. Ia terkenal menghantui kastel Uskup Bernhard dari Keuskupan-Pangeran Hildesheim di Niedersachsen; dalam sebagian versi ia menghuni Winzenburg dan menjadi roh kastelnya.
long_description.en: Hödekin (also Hödeken, Hütgin, Hüdekin or Hütchen) is a kobold or house spirit of German folklore. His name, a diminutive meaning 'Little Hat', refers to the pileus cap he wears. He is known for haunting the castle of Bishop Bernhard of the Prince-Bishopric of Hildesheim in Lower Saxony; in some versions he dwells at Winzenburg as its castle spirit.

long_description.id: Hödekin tidak memulai kejahatan, tetapi dendamnya mematikan: ia memotong-motong seorang bocah dapur yang terus menghinanya dan menuangkan kotoran dapur kepadanya, meracuni daging uskup dengan darah dan bisa kodok ketika juru masak mengeluh, lalu mendorong juru masak itu ke parit dari ketinggian hingga tewas. Namun ia juga menolong, misalnya dengan memberi juru tulis bodoh cincin daun salam yang membuatnya cerdas.
long_description.en: Hödekin did not start trouble, but his revenge was deadly: he cut up a kitchen boy who kept insulting him and pouring filth on him, tainted the bishop's meat with toad's blood and venom when the cook complained, and then pushed the cook into a ditch from a great height, killing him. Yet he also helped: for instance he gave a foolish clerk a ring of laurel leaves that made him clever.

long_description.id: Menurut Grimm bersaudara, ia mencegah penjaga malam tertidur, memberi uskup nasihat perang, memperingatkannya tentang bahaya yang akan datang, dan pernah diminta menjaga istri seseorang selama suaminya pergi. Masa tinggalnya di Hildesheim berakhir ketika uskup mengusirnya dengan mantra gerejawi. Jalan antara Winzenburg dan Domhof Hildesheim yang konon ditempuhnya untuk mengabarkan kematian Graf Winzenburg terakhir disebut "Rennstieg".
long_description.en: According to the Brothers Grimm, he kept the night watch from falling asleep, gave the bishop military advice, warned him of coming dangers, and was once asked to guard a man's wife while he was away. His time in Hildesheim ended when the bishop drove him out with ecclesiastical incantations. The road between Winzenburg and Hildesheim's Domhof, along which he reputedly ran to report the death of the last count of Winzenburg, is called the 'Rennstieg'.

role.en: A helpful but vengeful castle spirit.

famous_for.en: Haunting the Bishop of Hildesheim's castle.

did_you_know.id: Setelah menjaga seorang istri yang tak setia dari para kekasihnya, Hödeken mengeluh lebih suka menggembala semua babi di Sachsen daripada menjaga perempuan seperti itu lagi.
did_you_know.en: After guarding an unfaithful wife from her lovers, Hödeken grumbled he would rather herd all the pigs of Saxony than mind such a woman again.

note.en: Hödekin is a kobold.

statement.id: Hödekin dikenal menghantui kastel Uskup Bernhard (Bernhardus) dari Keuskupan-Pangeran Hildesheim di Niedersachsen; dalam sebagian versi ia menghuni Winzenburg, wilayah yang dibantunya diperoleh keuskupan.
statement.en: Hödekin is known for haunting the castle of Bishop Bernard (Bernhardus) of the Prince-Bishopric of Hildesheim in Lower Saxony; in some versions he inhabits Winzenburg, a county he helped the bishopric obtain.

claims.quote: Though Hödekin did not initiate harm, he was murderously vindictive. He dismembered a kitchen boy after the boy habitually insulted him and poured kitchen filth upon him. statement.id: Meski tidak memulai kejahatan, Hödekin pendendam yang mematikan: ia memotong-motong bocah dapur yang terus menghina dan menuangkan kotoran kepadanya, meracuni daging uskup dengan darah dan bisa kodok saat juru masak mengeluh, lalu mendorong juru masak ke parit dari ketinggian hingga tewas.
statement.en: Though he did not start harm, Hödekin was murderously vindictive: he dismembered a kitchen boy who kept insulting him and pouring filth on him, tainted the bishop's meat with toad blood and venom when the cook griped, then pushed the cook into a ditch from a great height, killing him.

claims.quote: Der Hödeken ist der Burggeist der Winzenburg. Er wird als eine zwergenartige Gestalt beschrieben (Kobold), die auch als Bote zwischen Hildesheim und Winzenburg Nachrichten übermittelte. Der Weg zwischen Winzenburg und Hildesheimer Domhof, den Hödeken nach dem Tod des letzten Grafen von Winzenburg entlanggeeilt sein soll, um die Todesnachricht zu überbringen, wird „Rennstieg“ genannt.

statement.id: Hödeken adalah roh kastel Winzenburg, sosok mirip kurcaci (kobold) yang juga menjadi pembawa pesan antara Hildesheim dan Winzenburg; jalan antara Winzenburg dan Domhof Hildesheim yang konon dilaluinya untuk mengabarkan kematian Graf Winzenburg terakhir disebut "Rennstieg".
statement.en: Hödeken is the castle spirit of Winzenburg, a dwarf-like figure (kobold) who also carried messages between Hildesheim and Winzenburg; the road between Winzenburg and Hildesheim's Domhof that he reputedly ran to report the last count of Winzenburg's death is called the 'Rennstieg'.

claims.quote: Der Hödeken war ein Geist, der sich am Hof des Bischofs von Hildesheim aufhielt. Er hinderte die Nachtwachen am Einschlafen, gab dem Bischof militärische Ratschläge und warnte ihn vor kommenden Gefahren. Gelegentlich half er auch anderen Hildesheimern. Einmal bat jemand den Hödeken, seine Frau während seiner Abwesenheit zu beschützen.

statement.id: Menurut Grimm bersaudara, Hödeken adalah roh di istana Uskup Hildesheim yang mencegah penjaga malam tertidur, memberi uskup nasihat perang, memperingatkannya akan bahaya, kadang menolong warga Hildesheim lain, dan pernah diminta menjaga istri seseorang selama suaminya pergi.
statement.en: Per the Brothers Grimm, Hödeken was a spirit at the court of the Bishop of Hildesheim who kept the night watch awake, gave the bishop military advice, warned him of dangers, sometimes helped other townsfolk, and was once asked to guard a man's wife in his absence.

claims.quote: He also helped an idiot clerk appointed to the synod by giving him a ring made of laurel leaves that granted him knowledge and intelligence. Ultimately, the spirit's time in Hildesheim ended when the bishop exorcised him with ecclesiastical incantations and drove him out of the city.

statement.id: Ia juga menolong seorang juru tulis bodoh yang diangkat ke sinode dengan memberinya cincin daun salam yang memberi pengetahuan dan kecerdasan; akhirnya masa tinggalnya di Hildesheim berakhir ketika uskup mengusirnya dengan mantra gerejawi.
statement.en: He also helped a foolish clerk appointed to the synod with a ring of laurel leaves granting knowledge and intelligence; his time in Hildesheim ended when the bishop exorcised him with ecclesiastical incantations and drove him out.

claims.quote: Als der Mann zurückkehrte, beschwerte sich der Hödeken: Er werde lieber alle Schweine von Sachsen hüten als nochmals eine solche Frau.

statement.id: Ketika lelaki itu kembali, Hödeken mengeluh bahwa ia lebih suka menggembala semua babi di Sachsen daripada menjaga perempuan seperti itu lagi.
statement.en: When the man returned, Hödeken complained he would rather herd all the pigs of Saxony than guard such a woman again.

claims.quote: „[…] auf dem Haupt trug er einen kleinen Filzhut, wovon man ihm den Namen Hütchen auf Niedersächsisch Hödeken gegeben hatte.“

statement.id: Menurut Grimm bersaudara, ia memakai topi laken kecil di kepalanya, sehingga diberi nama Hütchen, dalam bahasa Saxon Rendah Hödeken.
statement.en: Per the Grimms, he wore a little felt hat, whence the name Hütchen, in Low Saxon Hödeken.

long_description.en: Hödekin (variously spelled Hödeken, Hütgin, Hüdekin, and Hütchen, etc.) is a kobold (house spirit) of German folklore. The name, a diminutive meaning "Little Hat", refers to the pileus hat he wears, a style which was common in Ancient Greece and later various parts of Europe. Hödekin is known for haunting the castle of Bishop Bernard (Bernhardus), Prince-Bishopric of Hildesheim, located in Lower Saxony. In some versions of the legend, the spirit inhabits Winzenburg, a county which he helped the bishopric obtain. Though Hödekin did not initiate harm, he was murderously vindictive. He dismembered a kitchen boy after the boy habitually insulted him and poured kitchen filth upon him. When the cook (who hadn't controlled the misbehaving boy) griped, the sprite tainted the meat for the bishop with toad blood and venom. When the cook remained unfazed, Hödekin pushed him into a ditch from a great height, killing him. Hödekin's actions weren't always malicious. He once helped a man by fiercely protecting his wife. When the man jokingly entrusted his wife to Hödekin during his absence, the sprite took it seriously and chased off every man who called on the adulterous wife. He also helped an idiot clerk appointed to the synod by giving him a ring made of laurel leaves that granted him knowledge and intelligence. Ultimately, the spirit's time in Hildesheim ended when the bishop exorcised him with ecclesiastical incantations and drove him out of the city.

short_description.id: Bysen adalah makhluk hutan kecil dalam kepercayaan rakyat Gotland, Swedia, yang menyesatkan orang dan mengganggu para pekerja hutan.
short_description.en: Bysen is a small forest being in the folk belief of Gotland, Sweden, who leads people astray and plagues forest workers.

long_description.id: Dalam kepercayaan rakyat pulau Gotland, Bysen adalah makhluk hutan kecil yang memikat orang hingga tersesat dan menyusahkan para penebang. Siapa pun yang terlihat olehnya di hutan menjadi kacau penglihatannya sehingga tak bisa menemukan jalan pulang; penglihatan itu pulih bila ia membalik salah satu pakaiannya.
long_description.en: In the folk belief of the island of Gotland, Bysen is a small forest being who lures people into losing their way and troubles woodcutters. Anyone he catches sight of in the forest has their vision confused so they cannot find the way home; it returns to normal if they turn a garment inside out.

long_description.id: Ia menunda pengangkutan kayu dan menjungkirkan muatan kayu gelondongan, serta sering tampil sebagai tunggul pohon atau lelaki tua kelabu yang kecil dan tak mencolok, kadang bertopi rajut merah. Ia membawa kapak karena tugasnya menebang hutan Gotland, pekerjaan yang sangat lamban, kadang hanya satu pohon per abad. Ia dianggap manusia yang berbuat jahat semasa hidup dan dihukum mengembara selamanya, sekaligus penjaga hutan dan alam.
long_description.en: He delays timber transports and overturns loads of logs, and often shows himself as a stump or a small, unremarkable grey old man, sometimes in a red knitted cap. He carries an axe because his task is to fell Gotland's forest, which goes so slowly that sometimes only one tree falls in a century. He is held to be a person who committed a crime in life and is condemned to wander forever, yet also a keeper of the forest and nature.

long_description.id: Menurut sebagian sumber, bysar adalah orang mati yang dulu merebut tanah orang lain dengan memindahkan patok batas. Sebagai hukuman mereka tak tenang di kubur, berjalan di sepanjang batas yang salah sambil memindahkan patok dan bergumam "di sini benar, di sini salah". Bila seseorang mengikuti Bysen dan mengembalikan patok-patok ke tempat yang benar, Bysen mendapat kedamaian. Di daratan Swedia padanannya disebut skälvrängare atau osaliga lantmätare.
long_description.en: According to some sources, bysar are dead people who once seized others' land by moving the boundary markers. As punishment they find no rest in the grave, walking the wrongful boundary, shifting the stakes and muttering 'here is right, here is wrong'. If a person follows Bysen and puts the stakes back in the right places, Bysen finds peace. On the Swedish mainland the counterpart is called skälvrängare or osaliga lantmätare.

claims.quote: Bysen är i gotländsk folktro ett litet skogsväsen som lockar människor att gå vilse eller ställer till förtret för skogsarbetarna.

statement.id: Dalam kepercayaan rakyat Gotland (Swedia), Bysen adalah makhluk hutan kecil yang memikat orang tersesat atau menyusahkan pekerja hutan.
statement.en: In the folk belief of Gotland (Sweden), Bysen is a small forest being who lures people astray or causes trouble for forest workers.

claims.quote: Bysen försenar också transporter och välter timmerlass. Han uppträder ofta som stubbe eller en liten grå, oansenlig gubbe, och beskylls för allt möjligt ofog.

statement.id: Bysen menunda pengangkutan dan menjungkirkan muatan kayu; ia sering muncul sebagai tunggul atau lelaki tua kelabu kecil yang tak mencolok, dan dituduh atas segala kenakalan.
statement.en: Bysen also delays transports and tips over timber loads; he often appears as a stump or a small, insignificant grey old man and is blamed for all sorts of mischief.

claims.quote: Sometimes he wears a red woven cap and an axe because one of his tasks is to cut down Gotland's forest. This goes slowly, however, and sometimes only one tree per century is felled. It's said Bysen is a humanoid who has done some crime within his lifetime and is therefore sentenced to wander the Earth forever. Bysen is also the ward of the forest and nature.

statement.id: Kadang ia bertopi rajut merah dan membawa kapak karena tugasnya menebang hutan Gotland, yang berjalan lambat, kadang satu pohon per abad; ia dihukum mengembara di Bumi (Earth) selamanya atas kejahatan semasa hidup, dan juga penjaga hutan dan alam.
statement.en: He sometimes wears a red knitted cap and an axe since he must fell Gotland's forest, slowly, at times one tree a century; he is condemned to roam the Earth forever for a crime in life, and also guards forest and nature.

statement.id: Menurut sebagian sumber, bysar adalah orang mati yang merebut tanah orang lain dengan memindahkan patok batas antara dua bidang tanah; sebagai hukuman mereka tak tenang di kubur.
statement.en: According to some sources, bysar are dead people who tricked others out of land by moving the markers between two holdings; as punishment they get no rest in the grave.

claims.quote: Om en människa går efter Bysen och flyttar tillbaka de orätta gränsmärkena till rätt ställe, då får Bysen frid. På det svenska fastlandet kallas motsvarigheten skälvrängare

statement.id: Bila seseorang mengikuti Bysen dan mengembalikan patok yang salah ke tempatnya, Bysen mendapat damai; di daratan Swedia (svenska) padanannya disebut skälvrängare atau osaliga lantmätare, sementara mereka bergumam "Här är rätt, här är orätt".
statement.en: If someone follows Bysen and moves the wrong markers back, Bysen finds peace; on the Swedish (svenska) mainland the counterpart is called skälvrängare or osaliga lantmätare, and they mutter 'Här är rätt, här är orätt'.

claims.quote: Den som Bysen får syn på i skogen, får synen förvrängd, så att denne inte kan hitta hem igen. Den som drabbas kan, genom att vända ett plagg ut och in, återfå normal syn.

statement.id: Siapa pun yang terlihat oleh Bysen di hutan menjadi kacau penglihatannya sehingga tak bisa pulang; ia dapat memulihkannya dengan membalik pakaian.

long_description.en: Bysen (Swedish pronunciation: [ˈby̌ːsɛn]) is a legendary gnome-like creature that haunts the woods of the island of Gotland, Sweden. Bysen carries an axe. He is said to have committed a crime and condemned to walk the Earth forever. He attracts people, making them get lost. Often he meddles with foresters, delays their transports, and tips loads of timber over. He often interferes with men in other ways and is accused of all sorts of mischief. Bysen often appears as a stump or an insignificant, little, grey man. Sometimes he wears a red woven cap and an axe because one of his tasks is to cut down Gotland's forest. This goes slowly, however, and sometimes only one tree per century is felled. It's said Bysen is a humanoid who has done some crime within his lifetime and is therefore sentenced to wander the Earth forever. Bysen is also the ward of the forest and nature. Similar to the Deildegast from Norwegian folklore, some sources say that Bysen are deceased people who have cheated other men out of their land by moving the markers that separated two holdings. As punishment, they get no peace in the grave and are doomed to go along the faulty border, moving the sticks on the wrong land. As they walk, you can hear them mumble, "This is right, this is wrong", while moving the markers. If a human follows Bysen and moves the wrongly placed sticks to the right places, then Bysen will gain peace. On the Swedish mainland the counterpart to Bysen is called skälvrängare or osaliga lantmätare (approximately: unholy landsurveyor). If Bysen catches sight of you where you are in the forest, he will enchant your vision so that you can not find him again. What returns one's vision to normal is to turn a garment crooked.

short_description.id: Fasolt adalah raksasa atau kesatria dalam legenda heroik Jerman, dikenal dari Eckenlied dan Thidrekssaga, dan kelak menjadi tokoh raksasa dalam opera Das Rheingold karya Richard Wagner.
short_description.en: Fasolt is a giant or knight of German heroic legend, known from the Eckenlied and the Thidrekssaga, who later became a giant in Richard Wagner's opera Das Rheingold.

long_description.id: Fasolt (juga Fasold atau Vasolt) adalah raksasa atau kesatria yang muncul dalam puisi heroik bahasa Jerman Tinggi Pertengahan Eckenlied (sekitar 1230) dan dalam Thidrekssaga, kumpulan legenda Jerman berbahasa Nordik Kuno (sekitar 1250).
long_description.en: Known also as Fasold or Vasolt, Fasolt features as either a giant or a knight in the Eckenlied, a Middle High German heroic poem from around 1230, and in the Thidrekssaga, an Old Norse compendium of German legends from around 1250.

long_description.id: Namanya kemungkinan berasal dari akar kata yang mirip dengan kata Jerman Tinggi Kuno faso, "benang", yang agaknya merujuk rambutnya yang panjang dan dikepang dalam Eckenlied. Ia mungkin semula setan badai: sebuah doa abad ke-17 kepada para penyihir di gunung Jochgrimm dekat Bozen memohon agar "ffasolt" menjauhkan badai.
long_description.en: His name probably comes from a root akin to Old High German faso, 'thread', most likely pointing to the long braided hair the Eckenlied gives him. He may first have been a storm demon: a 17th-century prayer to the witches on Mount Jochgrimm near Bozen asks 'ffasolt' to send storms far away.

long_description.id: Dalam Das Rheingold karya Wagner, Fasolt dan saudaranya Fafner adalah dua raksasa yang membangun benteng Walhall bagi para dewa dengan imbalan dewi Freia, yang ingin dinikahi Fasolt. Atas desakan Fafner, mereka menerima harta Nibelung milik kurcaci Alberich sebagai gantinya; kutukan Alberich pada cincin itu memicu pertengkaran, dan Fasolt dibunuh Fafner ketika menuntut cincin itu.
long_description.en: In Wagner's Das Rheingold, Fasolt and his brother Fafner are two giants who build the fortress Walhall for the gods in return for the goddess Freia, whom Fasolt wants to marry. At Fafner's urging they accept the dwarf Alberich's Nibelung hoard instead; Alberich's curse on the ring sparks a quarrel, and Fafner kills Fasolt when he claims the ring.

The Old Norse compendium of German legends known as the Thidrekssaga (c. 1250). Richard Wagner's opera Das Rheingold (1869).
